name: Emeraude
lede: Emeraude is French for emerald, and as a color name it points less at the gem than at a green that French and English painters argued over.

sections.title: Two emerald greens
sections.body:
The Paterson dictionary glosses *emeraude* as simply the French for emerald, then adds that according to Maerz and Paul it is not the same green as emerald green [1]. The word hides a real confusion. In France *vert émeraude* named a transparent chromium green, while in English *emerald green* named a very different, poisonous copper green [2][3].

Our swatch is the Maerz and Paul color of 1930, which is the earliest record of the name in our sources [4]. It is a mid green, cooler and clearer than a leaf, and close to the cut stone it is named after, [[gem:emerald|emerald]].

sections.title: The French pigment
sections.body:
Pure chromium oxide had long been a dull pigment that painters did not much like [2]. In 1838 the Parisian colorman Pannetier developed a recipe that turned it into a deep, cool and slightly transparent green, sold in France as *vert émeraude* [2]. The chemist Guignet patented a process in 1859, and the dictionary adds that the pigment was discovered by Vauquelin in 1797 [3].

In England the pigment was called [[viridian]] [2][3]. The Impressionists adored it, and Ball calls it Cézanne's definitive green [2]. The Pigment Compendium warns that translators have often wrongly rendered *vert émeraude* as emerald green, a different pigment: copper aceto-arsenite, also sold as Paris or Vienna green, which was blamed in the 1860s for deaths from arsenic fumes in wallpaper [5][3]. The claim that arsenic wallpaper killed Napoleon is unproven, and not part of this story [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings this green appears in 36 paintings, 0.15 per cent, as photographed, rarer than 65 per cent of the named colors [6]. It peaks in the 1800s, at 2.0 times the rate expected from the same museums [6]. Its earliest strong match is in 1783, which is 147 years before the name's first record in our sources, so these are look-alike hues in aged photographs, not evidence of the French pigment [6]. Inside a painting it mostly plays an accent, in 57 per cent of 14 paintings [6].

origin.source: Paterson, Dictionary of Colour; Ball, Bright Earth ch. 15

disambiguation.gloss: the English pigment of that name is a copper-arsenic green, not the French chromium one

questions.q: What did the French call the pigment the English called viridian?
True or false: French vert émeraude and English emerald green are the same pigment.

openers: Vert émeraude and emerald green sound alike and are different pigments.

issues: all 8 claims verified (Paterson, Ball, Compendium); no changes needed
